name: "Be Like Mike"
annotation: The Gatorade campaign that turned a fadeaway, a tongue, and a shrug into the most imitated iconography on earth.
The season after the dynasty: the lockout Bulls went 13–37 and lost 82–49 to Miami. This is what breaking up the dynasty bought.

name: Air Jordan
annotation: $126M in year one against a $3M projection; by 1991 the brand did $1.3B. Fortune (1998) estimated Jordan's U.S. economic impact at $10 billion. A Black kid from Wilmington's sneakers became the world's uniform.

name: Allie Quigley
annotation: Franchise scoring leader until Vandersloot passed her (3,723 points). #14 retired July 9, 2025 — her wife Vandersloot, on crutches, gave the center-court speech.

name: Andrew "Rube" Foster
annotation: The founder. Outpitched white star Rube Waddell in 1902 and took his name; founded the Negro National League at Kansas City's Paseo YMCA on February 13, 1920, and ran it from Chicago. Committed to the Kankakee asylum in 1926, dead at 51 in 1930 — never seeing the back-to-back titles his team won without him. 3,000 mourners stood in snow and rain in Bronzeville.

name: Angel Reese
annotation: Drafted #7 in 2024, two All-Star seasons in Chicago, traded to Atlanta in April 2026 — then won 2026 Defensive Player of the Year with the Dream, setting single-season rebounding records. The one that stings.

name: Bernie Custis
annotation: The first Black quarterback to start professionally, for Hamilton in the CFL, 1951. America wouldn't; Canada would.

name: Bishop Bernard Sheil
annotation: Chicago's auxiliary bishop, who lent the Catholic Church's weight to the campaign in the Defender's pages, June 1942.

name: Branch Rickey
annotation: Signed Robinson to Montreal in October 1945. The executive who acted; the press corps who made acting unavoidable.

name: Caleb Williams
annotation: #1 overall, 2024. Seventy-one years after Thrower relieved Blanda at Wrigley, Chicago used the first pick in the draft on a Black quarterback.

name: Candace Parker
annotation: Naperville native, 13 seasons in LA, signed home in June 2021 and delivered the title. "I remember watching the Chicago Bulls' parade on TV and dreaming of bringing a title to your hometown." #3 retired August 25, 2025. Now Adidas president of women's basketball.

name: Cool Papa Bell
annotation: Center fielder, American Giants 1942. One of the fastest men to ever play the game, and one of thirteen Cooperstown plaques to wear this uniform. Hall of Fame, 1974.
notes: played_for St. Louis Stars · played_for Homestead Grays · played_for Kansas City Monarchs

name: Courtney Vandersloot
annotation: Drafted #3 overall in 2011; twelve seasons in Chicago, franchise assists queen five times over. Left, won a title in New York, came home in February 2025 — tore her ACL seven games in, but not before becoming the franchise's all-time scorer (3,745 points). Came back from the ACL at 37.

name: Cristóbal Torriente
annotation: Outfielder, 1919–1925; led the 1920 championship team with a .393 average. The Cuban star at the heart of the first dynasty. Hall of Fame, 2006.

name: Dave "Gentleman Dave" Malarcher
annotation: Foster's protégé who took over on-field management in 1926 and won both Colored World Series titles (1926, 1927) running Foster's pitching-and-defense pattern. The dynasty's second architect.

name: Dennis Rodman
annotation: Acquired before 1995–96; seven straight rebounding titles; the second three-peat's defensive engine and its cultural lightning rod. Exported his own model of Black masculinity entirely.
notes: played_for Detroit Pistons · played_for Chicago Bulls · played_for Los Angeles Lakers

name: Donovan McNabb
annotation: Started Super Bowl XXXIX (2005). Six Pro Bowls; the sustained-excellence case.

name: Doug Williams
annotation: Grambling; 17th overall in 1978, the first Black QB taken in the first round. Super Bowl XXII: 18 of 29, 340 yards, 4 TDs — all in the second quarter. 35 points in one quarter. First Black quarterback to start and win a Super Bowl.

name: Dwyane Wade
notes: played_for Chicago Bulls · played_for Miami Heat

name: Eddy Curry
notes: played_for Chicago Bulls · played_for Miami Heat

name: Elena Delle Donne
annotation: Drafted 2013; the 24–10 season, the franchise's first playoff run, the climb out of the 5–29 inaugural years.

name: Fay Young
annotation: The Chicago Defender's sports editor across five decades, credited as the first full-time Black sportswriter in America. Covered the Negro National League from its 1920 inception, built the Defender's sports page, and spent the 1940s demanding the majors open up. The Dean of Negro Sportswriters.

name: Frank Wickware
annotation: Threw a no-hitter on August 26, 1914, beating Indianapolis 1–0: walked the leadoff man, who was caught stealing, then retired 26 straight. The single-game masterpiece in franchise history.

name: Fritz Pollard
annotation: Brown, Rose Bowl 1916; led Akron to the 1920 league title; the NFL's first Black head coach (1921) and, with Hammond in 1923, its first Black quarterback. Purged with the color line; Hall of Fame finally in 2005, nineteen years after his death, on his son's dying quest: "Don't forget your quest."

name: George Mikan
notes: played_for DePaul Blue Demons men's basketball · played_for Chicago American Gears

name: Jackie Robinson
annotation: .376 for the Kansas City Monarchs in 1945; went 0-for-5 at Comiskey Park's East-West All-Star Game months before Rickey's call. Signed October 23, 1945; debuted April 15, 1947. The man the campaign was for.

name: Jalen Hurts
annotation: February 12, 2023: with Mahomes, the first Super Bowl with two Black starting quarterbacks — 100 years after Pollard.

name: James "Shack" Harris
annotation: 1969: first Black quarterback to start a season opener; the Times called him the "Negro passer." Roomed at a $6-a-night Buffalo YMCA while O.J. Simpson got the Hilton. 1974: first Black QB to start an NFL playoff game; Pro Bowl MVP.

name: James Wade
annotation: Head coach and GM 2019–2023; the third Black male coach to win a WNBA championship.

name: Jerry Krause
annotation: The GM who built everything around Jordan: drafted Pippen, traded for Rodman, hired Jackson. Said "players and coaches alone don't win championships" — Jordan quoted it back at him in his 2009 Hall of Fame speech.

name: Joe Bostic
annotation: People's Voice sportswriter; brought Black players to unscheduled tryouts at spring training centers.

name: John H. Sengstacke
annotation: Took over the Defender in 1940, walked into the owners' meetings as a publisher to make the integration case in person, and per a Congressional tribute helped arrange the Robeson meeting that preceded Robinson's hiring.

name: John Henry "Pop" Lloyd
annotation: Shortstop, 1914–1917, on the legendary 1910 Leland Giants team that reportedly went 123–6. The Black Wagner. Hall of Fame, 1977.

name: Justin Fields
annotation: 2021: the Bears' first Black starting quarterback in 68 years. The franchise's ledger, finally with a new entry.
notes: played_for Chicago Bears · played_for Pittsburgh Steelers · played_for Ohio State Buckeyes football

name: Kahleah Copper
annotation: 2021 Finals MVP. Game 4's closer alongside Quigley's 26 and Parker's 13 rebounds in the 80–74 title clincher.

name: Kendrick Nunn
notes: played_for Miami Heat · played_for Los Angeles Lakers

name: Lamar Jackson
annotation: Heisman winner told by a Hall of Fame GM to switch to receiver; refused to run the 40 at the Combine, forcing evaluators to watch him throw. 2019 MVP. After five TDs against Miami: "not bad for a running back."

name: Lamar Odom
notes: played_for Los Angeles Lakers · played_for Miami Heat

name: Lester Rodney
annotation: Sports editor of the Communist Daily Worker; the white press's rare ally in the campaign.

name: Lonzo Ball
notes: played_for Chicago Bulls · played_for Los Angeles Lakers

name: Marlin Briscoe
annotation: "The Magician." October 6, 1968: first Black starting quarterback in modern pro football. 14 touchdowns as a Broncos rookie — then Denver wouldn't let him compete at QB in 1969. Won two Super Bowls as a receiver instead.
notes: played_for Miami Dolphins · played_for Buffalo Bills

name: Michael J. Alter
annotation: Principal owner since inception; with Nadia Rawlinson (2023) steered the $85M valuation round — then the second-highest in the league.

name: Michael Jordan
annotation: Drafted 3rd overall in 1984. Five MVPs, six Finals MVPs, ten scoring titles, 63 points in a playoff game (still the record). Retired at 30 at the absolute peak, hit .202 for the Birmingham Barons, came back with two words — "I'm back" — and won three more rings.

name: Mule Suttles
annotation: First baseman and left fielder, 1929 and 1933–35; one of the great power hitters of Black baseball. Hall of Fame, 2006.
notes: played_for St. Louis Stars · played_for Birmingham Black Barons

Odell Beckham Jr.
notes: played_for Miami Dolphins · played_for Cleveland Browns

name: Oscar Charleston
annotation: Center fielder, 1919. Called by some the greatest all-around player in Black baseball history. Hall of Fame, 1976.

name: Patrick Mahomes
annotation: Super Bowl LIV MVP; the position's desegregation made dynasty.

name: Paul Robeson
annotation: Addressed baseball's owners at the December 1943 winter meeting urging integration. Under Landis's orders, they ignored him — not one question.

name: Pete Hill
annotation: Outfielder, 1911–1918, another pillar of the 1910 Leland Giants. Hall of Fame, 2006.

name: Phil Jackson
annotation: Head coach for all six titles. Installed the triangle offense and managed the Jordan–Pippen–Rodman–Krause tensions into a dynasty. Told before 1997–98 it would be his last year "even if you go 82–0."

name: Robert Sengstacke Abbott
annotation: Founded the Defender in 1905 on 25 cents and 300 copies, under the standing headline "American Race Prejudice Must Be Destroyed." Every Robinson story ran under that banner.

name: Rube Foster
annotation: The paradox: he built the Negro National League the Defender had spent 25 years covering — and the paper campaigned to integrate the majors knowing it would kill his league. It ran the campaign anyway.

name: Sam Lacy
annotation: Baltimore Afro-American sportswriter, one of the four Black press agitators who "took the lead in pushing baseball's establishment to hire black players."

name: Sandy Stephens
annotation: 1960: first Black quarterback to win a national title and earn All-American honors (Minnesota). Drafted by the Vikings and told he wouldn't play quarterback. Played in Montreal instead.

name: Scottie Pippen
annotation: The Robin without whom, by Jordan's own admission, the titles don't happen. Signed a seven-year, $18 million extension in 1991 — in 1996–97, his best season, he made $2.25M while Jordan made $30.14M. The wound that never closed.

name: Shaquille O'Neal
notes: played_for Los Angeles Lakers · played_for Miami Heat

name: Shedeur Sanders
notes: played_for Colorado Buffaloes football · played_for Cleveland Browns

name: Skytown (October 19, 2021)
annotation: The parade: Wintrust Arena up Michigan Avenue to Pritzker Pavilion. Governor Pritzker declared Chicago "Skytown" for the day. Chance the Rapper tried on a gold medal.

name: Smokey Joe Williams
annotation: Pitcher, 1914. One of the most feared arms of the era. Hall of Fame, 1999.

name: Space Jam (1996)
annotation: $230M box office, 6× platinum soundtrack. A Black athlete headlined a Hollywood film that taught the world's children his name.

name: Stefon Diggs
notes: played_for Buffalo Bills · played_for Houston Texans

name: Steve McNair
annotation: Started Super Bowl XXXIV (2000); co-MVP 2003. The bridge between Williams and the modern era.

name: Ted "Double Duty" Radcliffe
annotation: Pitcher and catcher, Giants debut 1929; named by writer Damon Runyon in 1932 after catching one game and pitching the next. Moved to the South Side in the Great Migration; died in Chicago at 103 — and at 96 became the oldest man ever to appear in a pro game.

name: The 2021 title run
annotation: 16–16, the sixth seed. Beat Dallas, Minnesota, then toppled #1 Connecticut 3–1. Finals 3–1 over Phoenix. Chicago's first pro basketball championship since 1998.

name: The 72–10 season (1995–96)
annotation: The first 70-win team in NBA history. Jordan won season MVP, All-Star MVP, and Finals MVP in the same year.

name: The Dream Team (Barcelona 1992)
annotation: Jordan and Pippen on the roster that won gold and globalized basketball, inspiring the generation of international stars who later remade the NBA.

name: The Last Shot (June 14, 1998)
annotation: Jordan over Bryon Russell to close the sixth title. 6–0 in Finals. No dynasty in modern sports closed cleaner.

name: Tristan Thompson
notes: played_for Chicago Bulls · played_for Los Angeles Lakers

name: Turkey Stearnes
annotation: Outfielder, 1932–35 and 1937–38, carrying the franchise into its later championship years. Hall of Fame, 2000.

name: Warren Moon
annotation: Undrafted 1978, told to switch to tight end. Five straight Grey Cups in Edmonton (1978–82), then the NFL: 1990 Offensive Player of the Year, nine Pro Bowls, both Halls of Fame. The exile cost him his twenties.

name: Wayne Edmonds
notes: played_for Notre Dame Fighting Irish football (University of Notre Dame)

name: Wendell Smith
annotation: Pittsburgh Courier sportswriter; his 1938 column told Black readers to stop spending money on teams that barred Black players — the boycott-logic template the whole press corps worked from. Later Robinson's traveling companion.

name: William C. Robinzine Sr.
notes: played_for DePaul Blue Demons men's basketball

name: Willie Foster
annotation: Rube's younger half-brother and the dynasty's ace: 26 wins in 1926 including 23 straight, then consecutive complete-game shutouts in a playoff doubleheader against the Kansas City Monarchs. Followed it with a 32–3 record in 1927. Hall of Fame, 1996.

name: Willie Mays
notes: played_for Birmingham Black Barons · played_for New York Mets

name: Willie Thrower
annotation: October 18, 1953, Wrigley Field: relieved George Blanda for the Bears — the first Black quarterback of the modern NFL era. Two games, then released. "Everyone knows the Jackie Robinson story; nobody knows the Willie Thrower story" — his son.

name: Willie Wells
annotation: Shortstop, 1929 and 1933–35, the defensive anchor of the 1930s clubs. Hall of Fame, 1997.

name: Wintrust Arena
annotation: Home since 2018, South Loop's McCormick Square, ~10,000 seats. The first real home after the UIC Pavilion and the Rosemont exile.
